title: Engineering Low-Latency, High-Throughput Quantum Decoders on NVIDIA GPUs
authors: Stefano Markidis, Luca Pennati, Ivy Peng
abstract: We design and optimize a quantum error correction (QEC) decoder for NVIDIA GPUs, combining Relay belief propagation, a state-of-the-art message-passing algorithm, with order-zero ordered statistics post-processing. Our implementation uses CUDA Graphs to control GPU execution, stops updates for converged samples, and collects unresolved samples in queues for post-processing. We optimize sparse traversal through coalesced message accesses, prefetching, and register reuse, and accelerate binary post-processing with warp-level collectives. In addition, mixed FP16-FP32 arithmetic and INT8 quantization reduce message storage and traffic while retaining accuracy using accumulators at higher precision. We evaluate surface, hypergraph product, and bivariate bicycle code workloads on NVIDIA A100 and GH200 data-center GPUs and a commodity RTX 5080. On the bivariate bicycle code at error probability 0.003, INT8 halves amortized decoding time relative to independently tuned FP32 with a negligible logical error rate increase on RTX 5080. With independent syndrome batches submitted back-to-back to concurrent decoder instances, RTX 5080 delivers 91% of GH200's highest measured throughput with an 8.9x shorter median submission-to-correction latency. The combination of performance optimization, mixed precision, INT8 quantization, and concurrent decoder instances opens a path toward QEC decoder clusters built from commodity GPUs.
summary: This paper presents a highly optimized, hardware-accelerated decoder for Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes running on NVIDIA GPUs. By combining advanced algorithms like Belief Propagation with aggressive optimizations such as INT8 quantization and CUDA Graphs, the authors achieve significant performance gains. The results demonstrate that commodity GPUs can be engineered into viable, low-latency clusters for future fault-tolerant quantum computing systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need for classical decoders for Quantum Error Correction (QEC) that can operate with extremely low latency and high throughput to keep pace with real-time quantum measurement data.
main_result: The combination of hardware optimizations, mixed-precision arithmetic (INT8), and concurrent processing allows commodity GPUs to achieve near state-of-the-art throughput while significantly reducing the median submission-to-correction latency.
method: The authors implemented a decoder combining Relay Belief Propagation (Relay-BP) with Order-Zero Ordered Statistics (OSD-0) on NVIDIA GPUs, optimizing the entire pipeline using CUDA Graphs and advanced low-level kernel techniques.
model_or_system: The work focuses on decoding syndromes generated by various QEC codes, including the surface, hypergraph product, and bivariate bicycle codes. The decoding process involves solving linear equations over GF(2) using message-passing algorithms.
key_observables: Amortized decoding time ($\mu s$/sample), logical error rate (LER), throughput, and submission-to-correction latency.
important_parameters: Error probability ($p \in \{0.001, 0.003, 0.005\}$), batch size ($B$), and the specific GPU architectures (A100, GH200, RTX 5080).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that independent syndrome batches can be submitted back-to-back to concurrent decoder instances, and that mixed-precision arithmetic maintains accuracy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the GPU decoding workflow using CUDA Graphs, the structure of the QEC check matrix (Tanner subgraph), and performance trade-offs between latency and throughput based on batch size and stream count.
paper_structure: The paper details the algorithmic components (Relay-BP and OSD-0), followed by extensive hardware optimization techniques (CUDA Graphs, mixed precision, quantization), and concludes with comprehensive benchmarking across multiple QEC codes and GPU platforms.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it directly tackles the engineering bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum computation by providing a roadmap for building scalable, high-speed classical control electronics for quantum processors.
